text: At 6pm your manager messages: "Can we talk tomorrow at 10?" — nothing else. What happens in your head for the rest of the evening?

options.label: My mind writes the worst-case script and plays it on loop — I barely sleep
A tight knot of worry; I keep re-reading the message hunting for clues
A flicker of 'uh-oh', then I distract myself and mostly let it go
Nothing much — I'll find out at 10, so I get on with my evening

text: You've waited twenty minutes in a queue and someone confidently strolls in right ahead of you. What actually happens inside?

options.label: Heat rushes up — I call it out sharply, and it sits in my chest for the next hour
A real flash of anger, though I keep my words measured
Mild irritation — I might say 'excuse me, there's a line'
I barely register it — not worth spending my mood on

text: Everything lands at once: a bill you forgot is overdue, your phone dies, and you're already running late. In that moment, what's the real you?

options.label: I freeze — it all feels like too much and I can't think straight
I get flustered and scattered, doing three things badly at once
Tense, but I pick one thing and just start
I go calm and methodical — pressure actually sharpens me

text: When a real disappointment lands — a rejection, a plan you cared about collapsing — how does the low usually move through you?

options.label: It pulls me under for days; I lose interest even in things I normally love
I sink for a while and it colours everything until it slowly lifts
I feel it fully for a day, then I start climbing back
I'm genuinely sad, but I return to myself surprisingly fast

text: Mid-meeting you realise you misread the task and said something confidently wrong, in front of everyone. Afterwards…

options.label: I replay the moment on loop for days, cringing every single time
It stings hard and I feel watched for the rest of the day
A hot flush of embarrassment, mostly gone by evening
I laugh it off — everyone has said something silly

text: Think honestly about your emotional weather across an ordinary day. Which is most true?

options.label: It swings — I can go from fine to really low or wound-up over small things
Fairly up-and-down; my mood tends to track whatever just happened
Mostly steady, with the odd dip I ride out
Remarkably even — people say I'm hard to rattle

text: It's Sunday after a week packed with people. An old friend calls: "Big group dinner tonight — come!" Your honest first reaction?

options.label: Yes! That's exactly the recharge I need — people light me up
Sounds good, I'll happily go
Tempted, but a quiet part of me is angling for a night in
I'd rather stay home — I'm peopled-out and refill best alone

text: Your friend group has been dithering over where to eat for fifteen minutes, going in circles. What do you do?

options.label: I take charge — 'Right, we're going here, decided.' I like steering
I put a strong suggestion on the table and rally people to it
I offer an option but happily step back if someone else pushes
I stay quiet and go along with whatever the group lands on

text: You're seated beside a stranger for a three-hour train journey. Left to your natural instinct…

options.label: I strike up a conversation easily — strangers turn into good chats fast
I'll warm up and talk if they open the door even a little
Polite hello, then I keep to myself unless they really persist
Headphones in — I quietly guard the solo time and don't engage

text: A friend proposes something spontaneous and a little thrilling — an impromptu road trip, leaving in an hour, no plan. You?

options.label: I'm in before they finish the sentence — I live for that buzz
Quick yes if I can grab my bag — that sounds alive
I'd want at least a rough plan first, then maybe
Not for me — I like my time calm and predictable

text: How would people who know you well describe your default energy?

options.label: A live wire — always doing, talking, on the move, upbeat
Energetic and sociable, usually the one keeping things moving
Balanced — I have my bursts and my quiet stretches
Low-key and calm; I move through life at my own gentle pace

text: Picture your room, your desk, and your phone screen exactly as they are right now. What's the honest truth about order in your world?

options.label: Everything has a place and stays there — mess genuinely stresses me
Generally tidy; I reset things regularly
Organised chaos — I know where everything is, even if others don't
Fairly cluttered — I tidy in bursts when it gets bad
Clutter honestly doesn't bother me; order just isn't my priority

text: You set a goal — the gym, a course, a side project. It's week three, the novelty's gone, and tonight you're tired. What usually happens?

options.label: I do it anyway — I've learned to act regardless of how I feel
I mostly push through; skipping feels worse than doing it
It's a coin toss, depending on how drained I am
I let it slide 'just for today'… and today keeps repeating
My good intentions rarely outlive the exciting start

text: You promised weeks ago to help a friend move house on Saturday. Friday night, a far more tempting invitation lands for the exact same time. What do you do?

options.label: I keep my word without a second thought — I said I'd be there
I honour it, even though I feel the pang of missing out
I'd try to do a bit of both, or line up someone to cover for me
If I can bow out gracefully, I'd probably take the better offer

text: When it comes to ambition and pushing yourself, which rings truest?

options.label: I'm driven — I set high bars and feel restless until I clear them
I work hard toward the goals that genuinely matter to me
I do solid, dependable work but I'm not chasing constant achievement
I'd take contentment and ease over striving any day — I don't need to climb

text: You spot something you really want that costs a meaningful chunk of money — say a whole month's spending money. How does the decision actually go?

options.label: I research it thoroughly, sleep on it, maybe weigh the pros and cons
I sit with it for a day or two before I commit
A quick gut-check, and then I decide
If I want it and I can afford it, I buy it right there and then

text: A new person enters your life — a colleague, a neighbour, a future in-law. What's your starting posture toward them?

options.label: I assume good intent and trust openly until they give me a reason not to
I lean toward giving people the benefit of the doubt
Friendly, but I watch and wait before I really trust
My guard stays up; trust has to be earned slowly
I assume most people have an angle until they prove otherwise

text: At a restaurant the waiter is slow, flustered, and gets your order wrong. Your whole table is watching how you'll handle it. What's the real you?
subDimension: agreeableness: treatment of people with less power

options.label: I stay warm and reassure them — everyone has rough days
Patient and kind; I point out the mistake gently, with a smile
I correct it politely, though a little coolly
I get visibly annoyed — I'm paying, the service should be right

text: A colleague you don't especially like is drowning in work and will clearly miss their deadline. You've finished yours. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to help without being asked — a person in trouble is a person in trouble
Ask if they need a hand, even if a bit reluctantly
Help only if they come and ask me directly
Stay out of it — their workload isn't my responsibility

text: You and a good friend both want the same thing — the last slot, the nicer room, the opportunity you're both after. What's your instinct?

options.label: I'll usually let them have it — their happiness matters more to me than winning
I look for a way we can both come out with something workable
I make my case fairly and let the stronger claim win
I go for it — I don't shrink from wanting what I want

text: A peer just landed the very thing you badly wanted — the job, the recognition, the praise. Underneath your congratulations, what's actually there?

options.label: Genuine happiness for them, no shadow — their win doesn't dim mine
Warm congratulations, with a small private pang I let pass
I'm happy for them, but the envy stings for a good while
It's hard not to feel it should have been me; I compare a lot

text: You hear that someone who once wronged you is now going through a genuinely hard time. What rises in you first?

options.label: Real compassion — I might even reach out; the past is the past
Sympathy; I wouldn't wish hardship on anyone
Mixed feelings — some sympathy, and a little 'well, that's karma'
Honestly, a quiet sense that they had it coming

text: Two weeks off, and the cost is the same either way. Which trip makes your heart genuinely lift?

options.label: A far-off country where I don't speak the language and nothing's planned — I want to be surprised
Somewhere new, with a loose plan and lots of room to wander
A comfortable, well-reviewed place with a solid itinerary
Back to the same place I love and know well — the familiarity is the whole point

text: A free evening, no obligations. Which pull is honestly the strongest?

options.label: A documentary, a deep article, or a rabbit-hole about something I know nothing about
A good book, or a conversation that makes me think
Something light and entertaining to switch my brain off
I'd rather not think much at all — comfort and rest

text: How much does art — music, poetry, design, a beautiful view — actually move you?

options.label: Deeply — a piece of music or a painting can genuinely stop me in my tracks
I appreciate and go looking for beauty; it matters to me
I enjoy it now and then, but I don't seek it out
It's not really my thing — I'm practical over aesthetic

text: You find yourself in conversation with someone whose worldview is the opposite of yours. What's happening inside you?

options.label: I'm fascinated — I want to understand how they got there; it might stretch me
Curious and open; I'm happy to hear them out properly
I listen politely, but mostly I'm waiting for my turn to disagree
I find it tiring — I'd rather be around people who see things as I do

text: How much do you live inside your imagination — daydreams, what-ifs, invented scenarios, ideas spinning off ideas?

options.label: A lot — my inner world is vivid and I spend real time wandering in it
Fairly often; I'm a daydreamer and an idea-generator
Sometimes, but I'm mostly grounded in the here and now
Rarely — I'm practical and present-focused, not much of a fantasiser

text: Walking through a near-empty parking lot at night, you spot a wallet on the ground. Inside: about 8,000 rupees in cash, an ID with an address, and some cards. No one saw you pick it up. Walk me through what you actually do.

options.label: Take the cash, drop the wallet somewhere someone will find the ID — the money's untraceable and honestly finders keepers
Keep the cash but hand the wallet and cards in — the person mostly needs their documents back, the money's a wash
Hold onto everything and tell myself I'll return it, but I know I probably won't chase it down
Return the whole thing intact through the address or nearest police station, even though it's a hassle
Return it all intact AND it wouldn't even occur to me to keep the cash — that money isn't mine, full stop

text: At the end of a long grocery run, you notice the cashier forgot to scan a 600-rupee item that's already in your bag. You're already at the door. What happens?

options.label: Keep walking — their mistake, their loss, the store won't miss it
Feel a flicker of guilt but leave; going back to pay MORE feels almost silly
Go back only if the item was expensive enough to matter; for something small I'd let it slide
Turn around and pay for it — the size of the amount doesn't change whether it's right
Turn around, pay, and quietly flag it so the cashier isn't short at closing

text: There's a way to save a real chunk of money that lives in a grey zone — under-reporting some income, an inflated reimbursement, a 'cash, no bill' deal that dodges tax. Technically wrong, extremely common, unlikely to ever catch up with you. Where do you land?

options.label: I do it without a second thought — everyone does, and the system's rigged anyway
I take the grey-zone option and feel fine; I only draw the line at things that clearly hurt a specific person
I go case by case — small stuff yes, but I get uneasy past a certain point
I mostly stay clean; cutting these corners costs me sleep more than it saves me money
I won't do it even when no one's watching and it's 'normal' — the rule applying to me is the whole point

text: Weeks ago you promised to help a friend move house this Sunday. Sunday arrives and something far more tempting comes up — a rare invite, a chance you'd hate to miss. Your friend would probably understand. What do you do?

options.label: Take the better offer and send a warm apology — a promise has to bend to real opportunities
Try to wriggle out with a half-true excuse so no one's actually let down
Show up but resentful and half-present, wishing I were elsewhere
Keep the promise because I gave my word, even though it genuinely stings to miss out
Keep it and mean it — once I've committed, the other option basically stops existing for me

text: Dinner out, and the waiter is slow, mixes up your order, and is clearly having a rough shift. The person across from you is watching how you handle it. What actually comes out of you?
subDimension: how they treat those with less power

options.label: I let them know firmly it's not good enough — I'm paying for a service and I expect it done right
Cold and clipped; I don't make a scene but I make my displeasure clear and skip the tip
Polite on the surface but irritated underneath, and I'll grumble about it after they leave
Patient — mistakes happen, I say it kindly and don't let it sour the evening
I notice they're slammed, cut them real slack, maybe ask if they're okay — how I treat them says more about me than about the food

text: Someone you quietly compete with — a cousin, a colleague, a batchmate — lands the big win you've been chasing: the promotion, the house, the recognition. The news reaches you. What's the honest first thing inside you?

options.label: A sour drop in my stomach, and I start privately picking apart how they didn't really deserve it
Envy I have to work to hide; I congratulate them but it feels forced
Mixed — genuinely a bit happy for them, genuinely a bit stung about myself
Real gladness for them first, and it nudges me to raise my own game rather than resent theirs
Clean, uncomplicated happiness — their win takes nothing from me, and I'll go celebrate it with them

text: Now the reverse: someone who once looked down on you, or beat you to something, hits a public setback — a deal falls through, they stumble badly. You hear about it. What's the real reaction underneath?

options.label: A quiet, satisfying 'serves them right' — I might even enjoy retelling it
A little flush of vindication I don't say out loud but definitely feel
Neutral — not glad, not sorry, it's just not my problem
A genuine pang of 'that's rough,' whatever happened between us before
Actual sympathy, and if there's a decent way to help without rubbing it in, I would

text: A decision you pushed for has clearly backfired, and it's cost the group real time or money. Everyone's now in the room figuring out what went wrong. What do you do in that moment?

options.label: Steer the story toward the circumstances and other people's parts — no reason to hang myself out to dry
Admit a sliver of it while making sure the bigger blame lands elsewhere
Own it, but only once it's obvious the trail leads back to me anyway
Say plainly 'this was my call and it was wrong' before anyone has to point at me
Own it fully, absorb the discomfort, and immediately turn to 'here's how I'll fix it' — no defensiveness

text: You check your bank balance and there's 50,000 rupees too much — a bank error, or a client double-paid. It might take them months to notice, maybe never. What do you do?

options.label: Say nothing and quietly enjoy it — their error, my lucky day
Spend it slowly while telling myself I'll sort it out if they ever ask
Leave it untouched and wait; if they come asking I'll return it, but I won't go out of my way
Flag it and return it fairly promptly — it isn't mine, even if keeping it were easy
Report it right away; holding money that isn't mine would bother me more than the money's worth

text: In a meeting, your manager praises a solution and credits it to you — but the real idea came mostly from a quieter junior who isn't in the room. Correcting it might dim your own shine. What do you do?

options.label: Take the credit and move on — visibility matters and they weren't even there
Accept it in the moment and maybe mention them later, one-on-one, if it comes up
Give a vague 'it was a team effort' that keeps the spotlight comfortably on me
Correct it right there — 'actually that was mostly [their] idea' — even if it costs me the moment
Correct it and make sure the junior hears about the praise directly; their growth matters more than my glow

text: You can genuinely help someone in a real bind — money, time, a connection — but in a way where they'll never know it was you, and no one will ever thank or credit you for it. How does that sit with you?

options.label: Honestly, if there's zero recognition I'm much less likely to bother
I'd help, but I'd want it to somehow get back to them that it was me
I'd do it if it's easy, but anonymous giving doesn't pull at me much
I'd help gladly; the anonymity is fine, the help is the point
I actually prefer it unseen — help that no one can trace to me feels the cleanest, most real kind

text: You told a small, convenient lie — nothing malicious, just smoother — and the other person has just realized it wasn't true and is looking at you. What's your move?

options.label: Double down and defend the lie — backing off now would look worse
Add a second little story to paper over the first
Get defensive and minimize — 'it wasn't really a lie, you're overreacting'
Come clean and apologize once I'm caught, a bit embarrassed but honest about it
Own it straight away — 'you're right, I wasn't honest, I'm sorry' — no scrambling

text: A group you're in starts warming up on someone who isn't there — juicy stuff, and you happen to know a detail that would make the story even better. Everyone's leaning in. What do you do?

options.label: Drop the detail — it's harmless fun and being the one with the good story feels great
Hold my specific detail back but happily enjoy and egg on the rest
Stay quiet and just listen without adding or stopping anything
Gently steer it elsewhere or say something fair about the person to cool it down
Say I'd rather not talk about them when they can't defend themselves — I try to speak the same about people present and absent

text: In a heated moment you said something to someone you love that genuinely wounded them. The heat has passed and you can see the hurt on their face. What happens next in you?

options.label: I wait for it to blow over on its own; apologizing feels like losing
I offer a quick 'sorry, but you also...' that's really about defending myself
I go quiet and warm back up gradually without ever quite naming what I did
I apologize properly for the specific thing I said, once I've cooled down
I go back, name exactly what I got wrong, ask what it cost them, and try to make it right — my pride comes second to the relationship

text: Your partner comes home unusually quiet tonight — short replies, eyes on their phone, not really present. Nothing has happened between you two that you know of. What is the very first story your mind writes?
subDimension: attachment anxiety (hypervigilance to a partner's mood)

options.label: 'Did I do something? Are they pulling away from me?' — I start replaying the last few days
A quiet worry that something is wrong between us, even as I tell myself to relax
I wonder what's up, ask once, and let it go if they say they're fine
'They've clearly had a rough day' — it barely registers as being about us

text: You sent a message that mattered to you this morning. It's now evening and they still haven't replied — and you can see they've been online. By now, what's actually happening inside you?

options.label: I've checked the phone a dozen times; a knot in my stomach that keeps tightening
Restless and a little hurt — I keep rereading my message wondering if it landed wrong
Mildly annoyed, but I assume they're swamped and will get to it
Honestly haven't thought about it much — they'll reply when they reply

text: After a real argument, the two of you fall into silence. Left to yourself in that space, what do you naturally do with it?

options.label: I go cold and shut the door inside — I genuinely need distance and don't want to be reached
I retreat into my own world; talking about it right now feels like too much
I need a little while to cool off, and then I want to reconnect
The silence unsettles me — I'd much rather we talk it through than sit apart

text: How often do you find yourself needing to hear — in actual words — that your partner still loves you and that the two of you are okay?

options.label: Often — when I don't hear it for a while, doubt quietly creeps in
Fairly regularly; hearing it settles something in me
Now and then, mostly during rough patches
Rarely — I tend to feel their love through how we are, not what's said

text: Someone you're close to wants more closeness than you're used to — more sharing, more time, more 'us.' What's your honest gut reaction?

options.label: A subtle urge to create space — too much closeness makes me restless
I appreciate it, but I also feel a little crowded and need to pace it
It feels good, though it takes me a bit to fully lean in
I love it — closeness is exactly what I want more of

text: At a family gathering a disagreement comes up, and your partner clearly sides with their parents — in front of everyone — leaving you standing alone. On the drive home, what's the loudest feeling?
subDimension: attachment anxiety (fear of being replaced / coming second)

options.label: A deep, aching fear: 'I'll always come second — I'm not really their person'
Hurt and shaken; I need them to reassure me tonight that I matter most
Stung, and I want to talk it out — but I don't really doubt where I stand with them
Disappointed in the moment, but secure that we're a team and we'll sort it privately

text: You're going through a genuinely hard stretch — health, work, or money. How comfortable are you leaning on your partner to actually carry some of it with you?

options.label: I'd rather handle it myself — leaning on someone feels like losing my footing
I'll share the headline, but I keep the heavy lifting to myself
I can lean, though I catch myself apologizing for needing to
I let them in fully — that's what a partner is for

text: There's a fear or a source of shame you quietly carry that almost no one knows. How does it feel to let a partner all the way into that?

options.label: I keep those doors closed — some things stay mine, even from a partner
I might hint at it, but fully opening up feels too exposing
I can share it, though it takes real trust and the right moment
Being fully known, soft spots and all, is exactly what makes it feel like love

text: In a relationship, how often does this thought visit you: 'I think I love them more than they love me'?

options.label: Often — I quietly keep track of who's more invested, and fear it's me
It surfaces in low moments and can really unsettle me
Occasionally, but it passes without much grip
Almost never — I assume we're mutual unless something shows me otherwise

text: Your partner says, warmly, 'I just need a couple of days to myself.' No conflict, nothing wrong. How does that land in your body?

options.label: Like a trapdoor opening — I immediately fear this is the start of them leaving
It stings, and I have to work hard not to read rejection into it
A small pang, but I understand and give it easily
Totally fine — everyone needs their own space, me included

text: You're clearly upset, and your partner moves in close to hold you and comfort you. In that exact moment, what do you tend to do?

options.label: I stiffen and pull back a little — being comforted like that makes me uneasy
I let them, but part of me wants to wave it off and say 'I'm fine'
I accept it, though it takes me a second to soften into it
I melt into it — being held when I'm low is a real relief

text: Your partner keeps talking warmly about a new friend or colleague — how funny they are, how easy to talk to. What's your inner weather?

options.label: A cold thread of insecurity — I start wondering if I'm being compared or replaced
A flicker of jealousy I have to consciously talk myself down from
A tiny twinge, but mostly I'm glad they've found a good person
Genuinely happy for them — it doesn't touch how secure I feel with us

text: Picture your ideal week once married. How much of it is 'me' — separate space, solo time, your own world left untouched?

options.label: A large chunk — I need substantial independence or I start to feel swallowed
A good amount; too much togetherness quietly drains me
A little pocket of solo time, but mostly I want our lives interwoven
Very little — I'd happily share almost everything and be together most of the time

text: Deep down, when you imagine really needing your partner — falling apart at 2am — how sure are you that they'll show up for you?
subDimension: attachment security (felt availability of the partner)

options.label: I'm never quite sure — I brace for being let down or left to handle it alone
I hope so, but there's an old doubt I can't fully shake
Mostly sure, with the occasional wobble
Completely — that certainty is the ground I stand on

text: You walk in after a genuinely rotten day — nothing went right, and you're rattled. Your partner is home. What actually happens with you?

options.label: I go quiet and disappear into myself — I can't talk about it until I've sorted it out alone, and that can take a day
I need some space first, then I'll come find you once I've made sense of it in my own head
It depends on the day — sometimes I want to talk it out, sometimes I just want to sit in silence next to you
Talking helps me think, so I'll start unloading almost right away, even if it comes out messy and half-formed
I have to say it out loud the moment I walk in — if I hold it in, it just churns louder

text: There's something you want from your partner this weekend — say, for them to plan a proper outing, just the two of you. How does that want usually reach them?

options.label: I drop hints and hope they pick up on it — asking straight out feels like I'm demanding
I mention it sideways first, and only spell it out if they completely miss the signal
I ask directly, but I wrap it gently so it lands soft
I just say exactly what I want — plainly, no packaging around it
I'm as blunt as it gets — I'd rather over-state it than leave a sliver of doubt about what I need

text: Your partner says "I'm fine" — but their voice is flat and something feels off. What's your honest instinct in that moment?

options.label: If they say they're fine, I take them at their word — I'm not a mind-reader
I might sense something's off, but I wait for them to bring it up on their own
I pick up on it and ask once; if they insist they're fine, I let it go
I can usually tell what's actually wrong, and I'll gently name what I'm sensing
I read the shift instantly — the tone, the shoulders, the pause — and I often know before they've said a word

text: Mid-argument, your partner says something that genuinely stings. In that very first moment, what happens inside you?

options.label: The sharp reply is out of my mouth before I've thought about it — I answer straight from the heat of the moment
I feel it flare, and some of that edge slips into my voice before I can catch it
I go quiet in the moment, mostly to keep myself from saying something while I'm hot
I feel the sting, but I can usually name it — 'okay, that one landed hard' — instead of firing back
I notice the anger rise, take a breath, and choose my next words on purpose

text: Your partner comes to you clearly upset about something — teary, deflated, or wound up. What do you naturally do?
subDimension: responding when a partner is hurting

options.label: I get uncomfortable with the heavy feeling and try to cheer them up fast so it passes
I go straight into fixing the problem — finding solutions is how I show I care
I listen for a while, then start offering suggestions on what they should do
I mostly just listen and let them feel it, holding back my advice unless they ask
I check what they need right now — a fix, a hug, or just to be heard — and I follow that

text: Your partner has a habit that genuinely bothers you — nothing huge, but it grates. How does that tend to come out of you?

options.label: I keep it in — pointing out their flaws isn't worth the tension it would cause
I hint at it or make a light joke, hoping they take the point without me having to say it
I bring it up gently at a calm moment, framed as how it makes me feel
I name it directly and fairly soon — things left unsaid only fester
I say it straight, on the spot — sugarcoating it would feel dishonest to me

text: The fight is over, you've both said your piece, maybe even half made-up. An hour later, where are you inside?

options.label: Still churned up — it can sit heavy in me for hours or even days, I can't just switch it off
I stew for a good while before I can properly settle
I need a little time, but then I'm mostly okay again
I calm down fairly quickly once I've had a moment to step back
I can reset within minutes — I really don't like carrying it around, so I put it down

text: You walk into a family gathering where, unknown to you, there's just been a quiet tension between two relatives. How quickly do you clock it?

options.label: Honestly, I'd miss it — people usually have to spell out for me that something happened
I'd notice a strong bad mood, but subtler undercurrents slip right past me
I'd sense the mood is off, though not always what's behind it
I'd read the room well and adjust how I show up to fit it
I feel the emotional temperature the second I walk in — I can usually tell who's off before anyone speaks

text: Something's gone wrong between you two and it needs to be talked through. What's the way you most want that to happen?

options.label: In writing — a long message where I can find the exact words and not be interrupted
I'd text to break the ice, then finish it face to face
No strong preference — whatever the moment allows is fine by me
A call or voice note — I need to hear the tone to know where we really stand
Face to face, always — anything written just gets misread and makes it worse

text: Your partner tells you, sincerely, that something you did really let them down. Before you even reply — what's your gut reaction?

options.label: My first instinct is to explain my side — I want them to see how it actually looked from where I stood
I feel put on the spot, and I reach to justify what I did
I feel myself bristle, but I make myself hear them out
I can take it in, even when it stings, and sit with whether they've got a point
I'd genuinely rather hear the honest version than be spared it

text: Think about how much of your inner world the people closest to you actually get to see. Which is most true?

options.label: I keep my inner world mostly to myself — even the people I love get the headlines, not the details
I'll share when I'm asked, but I don't often volunteer what's going on with me
I share the big things freely; the small day-to-day stuff I tend to keep
I think out loud a lot — you'll hear most of what's rattling around in me
I'm an open book — every thought, worry and half-formed idea tends to get spoken aloud

text: When something is quietly bothering you but you're not sure what, how well can you actually put your finger on it?

options.label: I just feel 'off' or irritable and genuinely can't name why
I know I'm upset, but pinning down the real reason is a struggle
Given some quiet time, I can usually work out what I'm feeling
I can name what I feel, and often what set it off
I read my own emotions clearly and can say exactly what's going on inside me and why

text: Your partner just did something that genuinely upset you — the anger spikes in your chest before you've even decided anything. In that first minute, what actually happens?

text: It's Sunday, you're finally with family, and your phone lights up — a work 'emergency.' Not life-or-death, but your boss is asking. What actually happens?

text: How much of your inner world — the worries, the hopes, the small stuff running through your head — does the person closest to you actually get to hear?

options.label: I keep my inner life mostly to myself — I process alone and share the conclusion, not the mess
I share selectively; I'm a fairly private person even in close relationships
The important things, yes — but a lot stays in my own head unless they ask directly
Most of it, once I've had a little time to make sense of it for myself first
Nearly all of it — I think out loud with them; they know what's on my mind almost in real time

text: In the marriage you'd actually want, how intertwined are your everyday lives?

options.label: Almost everything together — meals, errands, friends, weekends. We're one unit; I don't crave a separate life
Mostly shared, with the occasional solo outing thrown in
A healthy mix — plenty of shared life, plus our own friends and pursuits on the side
I need real independent space — my own hobbies, friendships, sometimes a trip alone — alongside our life together
I stay very much my own person in a relationship — serious autonomy and alone-time are non-negotiable for me, even happily married

text: You're both busy and apart all day. What feels right to you when it comes to staying in touch between morning and night?
subDimension: need for connection vs space (daily contact)

options.label: Frequent little messages and a call or two — I like feeling connected right through the day
A few check-ins — a good-morning, a couple of texts, sharing how it's going
A message or two is plenty; we'll catch up properly in the evening
I can happily go the whole day heads-down and reconnect at night without a second thought
I genuinely need to be in my own world during the day — constant contact drains me, however much I love them

text: Your partner has a warm, long-standing friendship with someone of the gender they're attracted to — regular chats, the occasional one-on-one coffee. Where do you honestly land?
subDimension: jealousy (trust vs threat in outside closeness)

options.label: I'm genuinely easy about it — their close friendships feel like part of who they are, and it doesn't unsettle me
Mostly relaxed — a small twinge might surface now and then, but it passes on its own
I'm comfortable when things feel open between us — being in the loop is what keeps me steady
I'll be honest, it sits a little uneasily — I'd probably want us to talk about where the lines are
That kind of closeness would be hard for me — I'd feel it in the background, and I'd want us to work it out together

text: When insecurity creeps into a relationship, which of these sounds most like the you that shows up?

options.label: I don't lean on constant proof — my security mostly comes from within, so this rarely troubles me
A bit of reassurance here and there steadies me, and then I'm genuinely at ease
I sometimes turn things over or want to know where I stand — I try to name it and talk it through
I notice I want to check in fairly often — who they're with, whether we're still okay
Insecurity can really take hold — I might ask for reassurance again and again, or feel a strong urge to look for proof

text: Picture your life ten years from now — where is 'home', the place you actually want to wake up in most mornings?

options.label: Right where I grew up — my town, my people, the streets I already know. I don't want to build my life among strangers.
A tier-2 city close enough to reach family in a few hours — familiar culture, calmer than a metro.
A big Indian metro — Bengaluru, Mumbai, Pune — that's where the opportunities and the life I want live.
Wherever my work and curiosity take me within India; I don't feel tied to any one city.
Abroad, or genuinely open to it — I want to build my life wherever the best life is, passport be damned.

text: Some people find one place and grow into it for life; others feel restless if they haven't moved in a few years. Which is truer of you?

options.label: I could happily live in ten different cities across my life — new places energise me and I don't need to 'settle'.
I like the idea of settling eventually, but I'd relocate a few times before I do.
One good move to the right city, and then I want to put down roots and stay.
I want to buy a home, plant trees, and watch the same neighbourhood age with me.
Roots are everything — same city, ideally the same community, for the rest of my life. Stability is the whole point.

text: When you imagine yourself at your most fulfilled, what does 'a life well-lived' actually look like?

options.label: A calm, contented life — enough money, good health, time with the people I love. I don't need anything grand.
A comfortable middle — a solid career and some recognition, but I won't trade my peace for ambition.
Steadily climbing — I want to be genuinely good at what I do, and known for it.
Building something that outlasts me — a company, a body of work, real impact.
Reaching the very top of my field, or leaving a mark most people never will — that hunger is core to who I am.

text: Life keeps offering a fork: a secure, predictable path, or a leap that could be brilliant or could fail. Across your life so far, which pull has been stronger?

options.label: Security, clearly. A stable job, steady income, a known future — that's what lets me sleep at night.
I lean safe, but I'll take a calculated risk when the downside is survivable.
A mix — one foot planted, one foot ready to jump when something exciting appears.
I'd rather try and fail than live a small, safe life quietly wondering 'what if'.
Big, bold bets are my natural mode — quit the job, start the thing, move the country. Uncertainty excites me.

text: Money and time are comfortable — no real worries. What does the good life actually look like, day to day?

options.label: Simple and light — a modest home, few possessions, no clutter. Less is genuinely more for me.
Comfortable but grounded — good basics, nothing flashy, savings over spending.
A nice home, good food, the occasional holiday — comfort without extravagance.
The nicer things — a beautiful home, real travel, quality in everything. I've worked for it and I want to enjoy it.
Big and abundant — a large home, the best experiences, a life that looks and feels expansive.

text: Be honest about your natural rhythm — not the one you think you should have. What pace does life feel right at?

options.label: Slow and spacious — long mornings, unhurried days, nothing crammed in. Rushing drains me.
Gently paced — some structure, but plenty of room to breathe.
A steady, productive hum — busy, but not frantic.
Full and fast — I like my days packed and my calendar humming.
High-intensity, always in motion — back-to-back, big goals, little idle time. Stillness makes me restless.

text: A home of your own versus the freedom to move — where do you actually land?

options.label: I'd rather rent and stay flexible — I don't want to be tied to a mortgage or a location. Experiences over property.
Owning would be nice someday, but not at the cost of chaining myself to one EMI or one city.
A home matters, but I can wait for the right time — I won't rush into a loan just to 'own'.
Owning our own home is important to me — it's security, and it's what a settled life looks like.
A house in our name is non-negotiable — it's the foundation you build a family and a future on.

text: When you're gone, what would make you feel your life had truly counted?

options.label: That I lived fully and enjoyed my one life — I don't need to be remembered for anything.
That the people close to me remember me warmly — that's legacy enough.
That I raised good children and left my family better off than I found it.
That I built or created something — work, an institution, ideas — that outlives me.
That I changed something bigger than myself — my field, my community, the world in some real way.

text: Fast-forward to 60. The version of that age that makes you smile looks like…

options.label: Peaceful and slow — a quiet home, grandchildren nearby, mornings with tea and the newspaper.
Comfortable and rooted — surrounded by family, community and familiar routines, no big plans needed.
Semi-retired and easy — some purposeful work, some travel, a gentle balance.
Still very active — new hobbies, real travel, learning, maybe the second act I always wanted.
Fully in motion — still working on things I love, still chasing goals. I never really want to 'retire'.

text: Two ways a marriage can run over decades. Which is closer to the life you want to share?
subDimension: togetherness vs autonomy in life vision

options.label: Two independent people with their own worlds, meeting in the middle — comfortable, low-friction, side by side.
Largely our own careers and lives, sharing a home and the big decisions, but not fused together.
A real partnership on the everyday things, with plenty of room for each of us to stay our own person.
Tightly woven — most days, dreams and decisions shared; we're a team in nearly everything.
One shared mission — we build a life, maybe something bigger, as a single unit. I want a co-founder for life, not just a companion.
